chapters.title: Chapter 3: India's Sovereign Debt Sustainability, Examined

lessons.title: India's Debt-to-GDP Picture: Centre, States, and Off-Balance-Sheet Liabilities

body.text: Ask three different sources for 'India's debt-to-GDP ratio' and you can get three defensibly correct but very different numbers, because the real question is never the ratio itself. It's what you counted to get there.

children.text: Earlier chapters flagged pieces of India's debt picture as they became relevant: the roughly 81 to 83% general government figure the IMF uses in its Article IV DSA, the DISCOM and subsidy-related contingent liabilities the IMF has repeatedly cited, and the weaker, more procyclical fiscal reaction function found at the state level. This lesson pulls all of that together and goes deep: how much debt actually sits with the Centre versus the States, what counts as 'off-balance-sheet' in India specifically, and how those liabilities have, in real documented cases, crystallised onto the government's own books.
Centre, States, and the General Government Number

stats.label: Central Government Debt
stats.context: The figure most commonly cited in Union Budget communications

stats.label: State Government Debt (combined)
stats.context: Compiled annually by the RBI across all states; varies significantly by individual state

stats.label: General Government Debt (IMF basis)
stats.context: Centre plus States, consolidated; the figure used in the Article IV DSA covered in Chapter 1

stats.label: Simple Sum vs Consolidated Figure
stats.context: Centre and State figures don't simply add up to the general government number, since intra-government holdings are netted out in the consolidated calculation

cells: Controller General of Accounts (CGA)
Central government debt and fiscal accounts
Union Ministry of Finance
Published monthly; the basis for the Union Budget's own debt figures
RBI, State Finances: A Study of Budgets
State government debt and fiscal accounts, consolidated across all states
Reserve Bank of India
Published annually, with a lag; state-level detail shows which states carry the heaviest debt loads
IMF World Economic Outlook / Article IV
General government debt (Centre plus States, consolidated)
International Monetary Fund
The figure used in almost every cross-country comparison and DSA discussed in Chapter 1

body.text: India's own official communications tend to feature the Centre-only figure, since 57 to 58% of GDP looks far more comfortable than the 81 to 83% general government number the IMF and rating agencies actually use in cross-country comparisons. Neither figure is wrong; they simply answer different questions. The discipline this lesson asks of you is to always ask which scope a quoted 'India's debt' number covers before comparing it to another country's headline figure.

children.text: When a Contingent Liability Becomes a Real One: The UDAY Scheme

body.title: DISCOM Debt, Before and After UDAY

events.title: Chronic DISCOM Losses Build Up
events.description: State-owned power distribution companies (DISCOMs) accumulate large annual losses and short-term debt for years, driven by underpriced power, high transmission and distribution losses, and delayed tariff revisions, none of which appears on the state government's own balance sheet while it stays at the DISCOM level.

events.title: UDAY: The Contingent Liability Becomes Real
events.description: Under the Ujwal DISCOM Assurance Yojana, participating states take over 75% of their DISCOMs' outstanding debt, as of September 2015, by issuing state government-backed bonds, converting a previously off-balance-sheet corporate liability directly into state government debt, in exchange for DISCOMs committing to specific operational and financial reforms.

events.title: The Losses Recur
events.description: DISCOM losses and debt build up again in several states within a few years of UDAY, showing the underlying problem, weak tariffs and poor collection rather than the debt structure itself, was not fully resolved, prompting further reform-linked borrowing incentives from later Finance Commissions.

body.text: This is the same underlying risk category as Mozambique's hidden loans and Zambia's opaque borrowing from Chapter 1, a liability that sits off the primary balance sheet until it doesn't, though India's version differs in one important respect: UDAY was a public, legislated scheme with disclosed terms, not concealed debt uncovered years later by surprise. The lesson generalises regardless of transparency: treating 'central government debt' alone as the full picture of a country's obligations is working from an incomplete number, whether the gap is hidden or simply sitting one level down in a state-owned entity.

children.text: Off-Budget Borrowing: The FCI/Subsidy Story and the 2021 Clean-Up

For years, a meaningful share of India's food and fertiliser subsidy bill was not paid for out of the budgeted fiscal deficit at all. The Food Corporation of India met a large part of its subsidy-related cash needs by borrowing directly from the National Small Savings Fund and through its own bonds, liabilities that sat on FCI's books rather than the Union government's, even though the government was always the entity ultimately responsible for repaying them. The Comptroller and Auditor General repeatedly flagged this as understating India's true fiscal deficit. Starting with the Budget for 2021-22, the government began bringing this off-budget borrowing back onto the explicit fiscal deficit calculation, a genuine transparency reform rather than a disclosure footnote.

body.label: The Scale of the Restatement
body.value: FY20 deficit restated from ~3.8% to ~4.6% of GDP
body.context: A large part of the jump reflects reclassifying previously off-budget FCI and other subsidy-related borrowing back into the headline fiscal deficit, separate from any change in the underlying spending itself

body.text: This is a smaller, domestic-institutional version of the exact blind spot covered in Chapter 1: an off-book liability that understated the true fiscal position for years before being brought back on the books. The difference from Mozambique or Zambia is not the underlying mechanism, it is that India's version was eventually self-corrected through its own budget process and CAG oversight, rather than surfacing only once a crisis forced disclosure.

children.text: NHAI and Government Guarantees: The Quieter Off-Balance-Sheet Items

body.caption: Other contingent and quasi-sovereign exposures worth tracking

cells: NHAI Off-Budget Borrowing
The National Highways Authority of India raises funds through its own bonds and market borrowing to fund highway construction under programmes like Bharatmala
NHAI's debt servicing depends partly on toll revenue and continued budgetary support; a shortfall would likely require the Union government to step in to avoid NHAI itself defaulting
PSU Bank Recapitalisation Bonds
A roughly ₹2.11 lakh crore recapitalisation package, announced October 2017 and implemented over FY18-FY19, issued 'recapitalisation bonds' directly to public sector banks

Recap bonds add to gross government liabilities without an immediate cash outflow, a technical mechanism, but the debt is real, and shows a banking-sector stress event landing directly on the sovereign's balance sheet
Government Guarantees to PSUs
Explicit guarantees extended to various public sector undertakings' borrowing
Sit outside the headline debt figure until and unless the guarantee is invoked, at which point they convert into real government debt, just as DISCOM debt did under UDAY

body.title: Draft the Real Number
body.scenario: You are drafting a one-page credit committee memo on India's sovereign debt. The Union Budget's own headline figure quotes Central government debt at around 57% of GDP.
body.prompt: What three items would you specifically ask for, or add back, before treating that 57% figure as India's real debt picture?
body.modelAnswer: First, state government debt, since the 57% figure covers only the Centre, and the figure that belongs in any real cross-country comparison, the one the IMF's own DSA uses, is the consolidated general government number, closer to 81 to 83% of GDP. Second, the current state of DISCOM and other state-level public-sector-undertaking debt that has not yet been formally taken over by a state government, since UDAY showed this kind of liability can and does crystallise onto a state's own balance sheet with little warning. Third, off-budget or quasi-sovereign borrowing sitting in entities like NHAI, since debt serviced by revenues that depend on continued government support is, in substance if not in strict accounting form, a government liability.

children.text: State Fiscal Rules and Reform-Linked Borrowing Space

Just as the Union government operates under the FRBM Act covered in the next lesson, every Indian state runs its own state-level Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management legislation, generally targeting a net borrowing ceiling around 3% of Gross State Domestic Product, a number the Finance Commission recommends and periodically revises. The 15th Finance Commission went further for the pandemic years, offering states additional conditional borrowing space, up to 0.5% of GSDP for FY21-22, specifically tied to undertaking power-sector reforms aimed at DISCOM financial health, alongside other reform-linked tranches. This is fiscal federalism deliberately doing what Chapter 1 showed discretionary fiscal reaction functions often fail to do on their own: using the incentive of extra borrowing room to force a specific, verifiable correction rather than hoping for one.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: India's Union Budget commonly cites a Central government debt figure of around 57 to 58% of GDP, well below the roughly 81 to 83% general government figure the IMF uses in its Article IV assessment covered in Chapter 1. What best explains this gap?
options: The IMF's figure is simply an error and should be disregarded in favour of the Union Budget's number
The general government figure consolidates Centre and State government debt together, while the Centre-only figure excludes state government borrowing entirely
India's states carry no meaningful debt of their own, so the two figures should be identical
The gap is entirely due to currency conversion differences between the two sources
body.explanation: The Union Budget's headline number reports only Central government debt. The IMF's general government figure, used in cross-country comparisons and in the Article IV DSA, consolidates Centre and State government debt together, and Indian states collectively carry roughly 27 to 29% of GDP in their own debt, which accounts for most of the gap between the two headline numbers.

children.text: A Field Checklist for Sizing Up India's Real Debt Picture

body.title: Before You Quote 'India's Debt-to-GDP Ratio'
steps: Start from the general government figure (Centre plus States), not the Centre-only number, for any cross-country comparison
Check the latest RBI State Finances report for which individual states carry the heaviest debt loads, since the state-level average hides wide variation
Ask specifically about DISCOM and other state public-sector-undertaking debt that has not yet been formally absorbed onto a state's own balance sheet
Check for off-budget or quasi-sovereign borrowing in entities like NHAI, and how much of its debt servicing genuinely stands on its own revenue versus implicit government support
Review the government's own guarantee book, published in Union and state budget documents, for contingent exposures that have not yet been invoked
Confirm whether the current headline fiscal deficit and debt figures already reflect known off-budget items, given the 2021-22 FCI reclassification, or whether new off-budget items have since emerged

body.text: This lesson explains how to disaggregate and interpret India's public debt figures for educational purposes only. It is not investment advice. Debt ratios, restated fiscal deficit figures, and scheme details are approximate and change with each data release; always verify against the current Union Budget, CGA, RBI, and CAG publications before relying on a specific figure.

points: India's Centre-only debt (~57-58% of GDP) and the IMF's general government figure (~81-83% of GDP, Centre plus States) are both correct but answer different questions; always check which scope a quoted number covers

UDAY (2015) is a real, documented case of a contingent liability, DISCOM debt, crystallising into actual state government debt, and DISCOM losses recurred afterward, showing the underlying problem outlasted the one-off fix

India's own off-budget FCI/subsidy borrowing understated the true fiscal deficit for years, a domestic version of Chapter 1's hidden-debt blind spot, resolved through a genuine 2021-22 transparency reform
NHAI's off-budget borrowing, PSU bank recapitalisation bonds, and government guarantees are quieter but real contingent exposures that sit outside the headline debt figure until triggered

State-level fiscal rules and reform-linked conditional borrowing space (as under the 15th Finance Commission) are a concrete example of using incentives to force the fiscal correction that Chapter 1 showed discretionary judgment often fails to deliver alone
